content.title: About
content.content: Banana pudding is a dessert made from ripe bananas, milk, eggs, sugar, and cookies (usually vanilla wafers or ladyfingers). The mixture is baked or steamed, then chilled until it reaches a thick, creamy consistency. It features a delicate banana aroma, sweet flavor, and soft texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Banana pudding is especially popular in the Southern United States, notably in Louisiana, where it is often served as a “banana cobbler” style dessert.
Traditional recipes use vanilla wafers that soak up the custard, creating a characteristic “soggy” layer.
Over‑ripe bananas are preferred for maximum sweetness and aroma.
Variations may include caramel, nuts, whipped cream, or even a splash of rum or bourbon.
Banana pudding is frequently served in individual glasses, topped with whipped cream and banana slices.

items.title: Rich in potassium
items.content: Bananas provide a high amount of potassium, which supports normal blood pressure and muscle function.

items.title: Source of vitamin B6
items.content: Vitamin B6 is involved in protein metabolism and neurotransmitter synthesis.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber from bananas and cookies aids healthy digestion.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: When made with low‑fat milk, the pudding contains little saturated fat, making it more heart‑friendly.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Bananas contain vitamin C and other antioxidants that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Milk or egg allergy
items.content: People allergic to dairy or eggs should use suitable alternatives.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Traditional pudding contains a fair amount of sugar; those with diabetes should monitor portion size.

items.title: Calorie density
items.content: Because of cream, sugar, and cookies, the dessert can be calorie‑dense, so moderation is advised.

items.title: Choking hazard for children
items.content: Small cookie pieces may pose a choking risk for young children.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve banana pudding chilled in individual glasses or bowls. Top with whipped cream, caramel sauce, nuts, or fresh banana slices. It also works well layered in parfait glasses.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep banana pudding in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. Chill before serving. Discard if it develops an off‑smell or excess liquid.

content.title: About
content.content: Reduced‑fat bologna is a cooked sausage made from beef, pork and turkey with a lowered fat content (about 5 %). The product has a mild flavor, a characteristic smoked aroma and a pink color. It is commonly used in sandwiches, salads and as a snack.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Bologna originates from the Italian city of Bologna, where traditional sausage was made from beef and pork.
The reduced‑fat version is achieved by adding lean meat and trimming excess fat.
Compared with classic bologna, the low‑fat variant contains fewer calories while retaining most of the protein.
Bologna is popular in diet plans because it slices easily and cooks quickly.
The product can be smoked or simply cooked; ours is cooked without additional smoking.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Bologna provides about 15 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: Low fat content
items.content: The reduced fat level makes it suitable for calorie‑controlled diets.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: It contains vitamin B12, niacin and riboflavin, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Contains iron and zinc
items.content: These minerals support immune function and blood formation.

items.title: Low carbohydrate
items.content: Practically no carbs, which fits well with low‑carb eating plans.

items.title: Meat allergy
items.content: Some individuals may have allergic reactions to beef or pork.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Like most processed meats, bologna contains a notable amount of salt; people with hypertension should monitor portions.

items.title: Preservatives
items.content: Certain batches may contain nitrites or other preservatives that are not suitable for everyone.

items.title: Storage safety
items.content: The product should be kept refrigerated and consumed within a few days after opening to prevent bacterial growth.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Slice bologna thinly for sandwiches, add it to salads, make hot subs, or use it as a filling for wraps. It can also be quickly warmed in the microwave or on a skillet.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store bologna in its original packaging in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C. After opening, tightly wrap in cling film or transfer to an airtight container. Use within 5–7 days.

content.title: About
content.content: The chicken deli sandwich (or sub) is a sandwich that features tender marinated chicken breast, fresh vegetables, cheese, and sauce, placed inside a soft roll or a long baguette. It is commonly served in fast‑casual restaurants and cafés.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The chicken in a deli sandwich is often marinated in a blend of soy sauce, honey, and spices.
A "sub" is an American term for a long sandwich, frequently layered with multiple fillings.
Some venues add crispy bacon or avocado to boost flavor.
Chicken deli subs are popular in summer menus because of their light taste.
The original recipe often uses a whole‑grain roll, increasing its nutritional value.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Chicken breast provides high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Compared with red meat, chicken contains less saturated fat, making it more heart‑friendly.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Chicken is a good source of niacin (B3) and vitamin B6, which support metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: The sandwich supplies phosphorus, selenium, and zinc, important for bones and immunity.

items.title: Fiber from vegetables
items.content: Fresh veggies add dietary fiber that aids digestion.

items.title: Chicken allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to chicken.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Marinades and sauces can be high in salt; people with hypertension should watch portion size.

items.title: Cross‑contamination
items.content: Proper handling is essential to avoid contact with raw meat and prevent foodborne illness.

items.title: Gluten in the roll
items.content: Traditional rolls contain wheat; a gluten‑free alternative is needed for those with celiac disease.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The sandwich is usually served cut in half and can be eaten with hands or with a fork and knife. It pairs well with fries, a side salad, or a light yogurt‑based sauce.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Best enjoyed fresh. If you need to store it, wrap tightly in plastic film and keep refrigerated for up to 24 hours. Store the roll in a dry place and keep cooked chicken in an airtight container.

quesadilla-beef-or-pork-with-vegetables.title: Quesadilla, beef or pork, with vegetables

content.title: About
content.content: A quesadilla is a Mexican dish consisting of a thin corn or flour tortilla filled with meat (beef or pork), vegetables, and cheese, then toasted until golden and crispy. It is popular both as street food and in fast‑casual restaurants.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Traditionally quesadillas are cooked on a hot griddle or skillet without added oil.
The word “quesadilla” derives from the Spanish “queso,” meaning cheese.
There are many regional variations in Mexico, some using fish, chicken, or only vegetables.
Quesadillas are commonly served with salsa, guacamole, and sour cream.
In the United States their popularity surged in the 1990s thanks to fast‑food chains.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Beef or pork provides high‑quality animal protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: The meat supplies vitamin B12, niacin, and riboflavin, supporting energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Contains vegetables
items.content: Bell peppers, onions, and tomatoes add vitamin C, fiber, and antioxidants.

items.title: Calcium from cheese
items.content: Melted cheese contributes calcium, important for bone and teeth health.

items.title: Moderate healthy fats
items.content: When prepared without excess oil, the dish contains mainly monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fats from meat and cheese.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: Because of cheese and meat, quesadillas can be calorie‑dense; portion control is advisable for weight management.

items.title: Sodium
items.content: Cheese and ready‑made sauces often contain a lot of salt, which may be problematic for hypertension.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: People with lactose intolerance or milk protein allergy should choose dairy‑free alternatives.

items.title: Food‑borne illness risk
items.content: Undercooked meat can harbor pathogenic bacteria; ensure the filling reaches a safe internal temperature.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cut the quesadilla into wedges and serve hot, typically with salsa, guacamole, sour cream, or a squeeze of lime. Fresh herbs such as cilantro can be added for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. Reheat in a skillet or grill to restore crispness.

content.title: About
content.content: Rice is a cereal grain harvested from the plant Oryza sativa. White rice is polished to remove the husk and bran, while wild rice (Zizania) is a distinct species with higher protein and fiber. When cooked, both become tender, aromatic, and easily digestible.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: White rice is a staple food for more than half of the world’s population.
Wild rice contains more protein and micronutrients than typical white rice.
In Japan, rice is central to rituals and dishes such as sushi and okonomiyaki.
Rice readily absorbs flavors, which is why it is often cooked with broth, spices, or vegetables.
There are over 40,000 rice varieties, differing in color, aroma, and texture.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Rice is rich in carbohydrates that quickly convert to glucose, providing the body with fuel.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Cooked rice contains virtually no fat, making it suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Rice provides thiamine (B1), niacin (B3) and vitamin B6, which support metabolism.

items.title: Provides minerals
items.content: Magnesium, phosphorus and iron in rice help maintain muscle function and blood health.

items.title: Hypoallergenic
items.content: Rice rarely triggers allergic reactions, so it is often used in infant and hypoallergenic diets.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: White rice can cause rapid spikes in blood sugar, which may be problematic for diabetics.

items.title: Low fiber content
items.content: Unlike whole‑grain foods, white rice provides little dietary fiber.

items.title: Arsenic accumulation
items.content: Rice can absorb arsenic from soil; rinsing and cooking in excess water reduces levels.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Rice can be served as a side dish, added to soups, salads, pilafs, sushi, or made into porridge. For richer flavor, cook it in broth, add herbs, spices, vegetables, or legumes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dry rice in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. Cooked rice should be cooled quickly and kept in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days, or frozen for longer storage.

content.title: About
content.content: Soup, sopa de fideo aguada is a traditional Mexican broth made with thin wheat noodles (fideo) cooked in a light vegetable or chicken stock. The dish is served hot, often garnished with fresh herbs, lime wedges, and sometimes a spicy sauce.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The dish originated in central Mexico and is commonly served as a light lunch or snack.
Fideo is a thin wheat noodle similar to vermicelli.
It is traditionally cooked in large pots over an open flame, giving it a characteristic smoky aroma.
Variations may include chicken, beef, beans, or corn added to the broth.
Typical garnishes are fresh cilantro, lime slices, and crunchy tortilla chips.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: A broth‑based soup with noodles provides few calories, making it suitable for weight‑management diets.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Wheat noodles supply B1, B3, and folate, which support metabolic processes.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: The high liquid content helps maintain proper hydration.

items.title: Easy to digest
items.content: Soft texture and mild ingredients make the soup gentle on the stomach, suitable for children and seniors.

items.title: Contains minerals
items.content: Bone‑based broths add calcium, magnesium, and phosphorus.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Prepared broth can be salty; people with hypertension should monitor added salt.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: Traditional fideo contains wheat, making the dish unsuitable for those with celiac disease.

items.title: Meat allergies
items.content: If chicken or beef is added, allergic individuals should avoid the soup.

items.title: Spicy additives
items.content: Chili and hot sauces may irritate the stomach of people with gastritis or ulcers.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the soup hot in a deep bowl, adding fresh cilantro, a squeeze of lime, and optional crunchy tortilla chips. For a heartier version, include shredded chicken, beef, or vegetables.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in portion‑sized containers for up to 2 months after cooling.
